read.sections.0.text.source: In 1950, a British scientist called Alan Turing asked, “Can machines think?” Then, computers were new, huge and slow, and very few places had one. On 31 August 1955, four researchers in the United States wrote a proposal. Two worked at a college and a university, and two worked at big companies. They asked for 10 people to study “artificial intelligence” together for two months. They hoped to find out how machines could use language, form ideas, solve problems and get better by themselves. They believed one summer could bring real progress. The researchers asked a private charity, the Rockefeller Foundation, for money, and it agreed. The project took place at Dartmouth College in 1956. It did not solve those problems. But the name from the proposal is still used today.
read.sections.0.text.back: In 1950 an English scientist named Alan Turing asked “Can machines think?” At that time computers were still new, very large and slow, and only a few places had them. On 31 August 1955 four researchers in the United States wrote a proposal. Two worked at a college and university, and two worked at big companies. They asked for 10 people to study “artificial intelligence” together for two months. They hoped to find out how machines could use language, form ideas, solve problems and get better by themselves. They believed one summer could bring real progress. The researchers asked for money from a private charity called the Rockefeller Foundation, and the foundation agreed. The project took place at Dartmouth College in 1956 and did not solve those problems, but the name that came from that proposal is still used today.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: In 1950, a British scientist, Alan Turing, asked: can machines think? Computers were new, huge and slow. In 1955, four researchers wrote a plan. This proposal asked for 10 people to work for two months. They would study “artificial intelligence”. Could machines use language? Could they solve problems and get better on their own? The group hoped to do a lot in one summer. A charity, the Rockefeller Foundation, paid. The project was at Dartmouth College in 1956. It did not solve these problems. But we still use its name.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: In 1950 an English scientist named Alan Turing asked: can machines think? Then computers were still new, very big and slow. In 1955 four researchers wrote a plan. This proposal asked for 10 people to work for two months. They would study “artificial intelligence”. Can machines use language? Can they solve problems and get better by themselves? The group hoped to do a lot in one summer. A charity called the Rockefeller Foundation paid. In 1956 the project was held at a college named Dartmouth. It did not solve these problems, but we still use its name.

read.sections.1.text.source: After 1956, researchers tried different ideas at the same time. Some wrote rules for computers to follow. Others built machines that learn from examples, like the perceptron, shown by the US Navy in 1958. Much of the money came from governments. In the United States, a military agency paid for AI work at universities such as MIT and Stanford. Some researchers made big promises, but real problems were harder than expected. Computers were slow, and there was little data. In 1973, a British report criticised much AI research, and Britain then cut funding for some of it. Expert systems, built from rules that experts gave, began in the 1960s. In the 1980s, companies and governments, including Japan's, spent a lot on them. These cost a lot to keep up, and their market fell in the late 1980s. Times like these, when money and interest fell, are called AI winters. Historians still argue about their exact dates and causes.
read.sections.1.text.back: After 1956 researchers tried many ideas at the same time. Some wrote rules for computers to follow. Some built machines that learn from examples, such as the perceptron the US Navy showed in 1958. Much of the money came from governments. In the United States a military agency paid for AI work at universities such as MIT and Stanford. Some researchers made big promises, but the real problems turned out harder than expected. Computers were still slow and there was little data. In 1973 a British report criticised much AI research, and Britain then cut funding for some work. Expert systems, built from rules that experts gave, began in the 1960s. By the 1980s companies and governments, including Japan's government, spent a lot on these systems. But they were costly to look after, and their market fell in the late 1980s. A period like this when money and interest fall is called an AI winter. Historians still argue about when these periods began and ended and what caused them.
read.sections.1.text.note: Reviewer: Much of the money: เงินส่วนใหญ่ (most of the money) changed to เงินจำนวนมาก, as in the English.

In the 1980s, firms paid for expert systems. These used rules from experts. They cost a lot to keep up. Their market fell in the late 1980s. These slow times are called AI winters. read.sections.2.heading.source: Data, chips and the return of learning
read.sections.2.heading.back: Data, chips and the return of learning

read.sections.2.text.source: AI is one part of a bigger story. Computers, the internet and digital data each have their own history. AI needed all three. There were also big successes. In 1997, a chess computer called Deep Blue beat the world champion, Garry Kasparov, though it could only play chess. Machine learning, an idea from the 1950s, grew much stronger after 2010. The internet helped researchers collect millions of labelled photos, and graphics chips made the work faster. In 2012, a team at a university built a program that was much better at naming things in photos. Rules did not go away. Many tools today mix rules and learning. Today, teams in many places build AI, also in Southeast Asia.
read.sections.2.text.back: AI is part of a bigger story. Computers, the internet and digital data each have their own history, and AI needs all three. There were also big successes. In 1997 a chess computer named Deep Blue beat world champion Garry Kasparov, even though it could only play chess. Machine learning, an idea from the 1950s, became much stronger after 2010. The internet helped researchers collect millions of labelled photos, and graphics chips made the work faster. In 2012 a university team built a program that named things in photos much better than before. Rules did not disappear: many tools today use both rules and learning. Today teams in many places build AI, including in Southeast Asia.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Turing's life outside this paper (his wartime work and how he was treated later) is told in films and books, and some learners may know of it. This lesson leaves it out. If it comes up, keep it brief and factual, and don't ask learners about anyone's personal life.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: Turing's life beyond this paper (his wartime work, and how he was treated later) is told in films and books, and some learners may know it. This lesson does not cover it. If someone asks, answer briefly and factually, and do not ask learners about anyone's private life.

educatorNotes.0.source: For teachers who want more: from the 1960s to the 1990s, DARPA, a US military research agency, gave most US government money for AI research, at MIT, Stanford, Carnegie Mellon and elsewhere (National Research Council, 1999). The Lighthill report was submitted in March 1972 and published in 1973; it is often said to have caused Britain's first AI winter, but Agar (BJHS, 2020; link in the claim record) shows the Science Research Council then funded some kinds of AI and not others. Haigh (2024) argues the deeper winter came in the late 1980s, after an expert-systems boom that Japan's Fifth Generation project and DARPA's Strategic Computing Initiative helped pay for; Japan ended its project in 1992 (Computer History Museum).
educatorNotes.0.back: For teachers who want to know more: from the 1960s to the 1990s DARPA, the US military research agency, gave most of the US government's money for AI research at MIT, Stanford, Carnegie Mellon and elsewhere (National Research Council, 1999). The Lighthill report was submitted in March 1972 and published in 1973. People often say it caused the first AI winter in Britain, but Agar (BJHS, 2020; link in the claims log) shows the Science Research Council at the time still funded some kinds of AI but not others. Haigh (2024) argues that the harsher winter came in the late 1980s after the expert-system boom, which Japan's Fifth Generation project and DARPA's Strategic Computing Initiative helped fund. Japan ended the project in 1992 (Computer History Museum).

educatorNotes.1.source: The evidence is real: the Dartmouth proposal (31 August 1955; the $7,500 Rockefeller grant, and industry researchers paid by their firms, come from the National Research Council's 1999 history, not the proposal) and a dated timeline. Teach the proposal's hopes, the people and institutions behind it and who paid, not names and dates to memorise. Its own topics already put “neuron nets” (learning) beside programs that follow rules: the approaches overlapped from the start. A possible discussion: why might confident plans help researchers win money, and what happens when the results come more slowly?
educatorNotes.1.back: This evidence is real: the Dartmouth proposal (31 August 1955; the 7,500 US dollar Rockefeller grant and the companies paying their own researchers come from the National Research Council's 1999 history, not from the proposal) and the dated timeline. Teach the proposal's hopes, the people and institutions behind it, and who paid, not names and dates to memorise. The proposal's own topics already put “neuron nets” (learning) next to rule-following programs: the two approaches overlapped from the start. Possible discussion: why a confident-sounding plan might help researchers get funding, and what happens when results come later than expected?
